pr_title: Make Searchable Snapshot's CacheFile Lock less
pr_body:
Replacing the mechanism for eviction and listener references via a read-write lock by
a reference counting implementation.
This fixes a bug that caused test failure #63586 in which concurrently trying to acquire or release
an eviction listener while doing a file operation would sometimes lead to throwing an exception
since the `tryLock` call on the read lock would fail in this case.
Also this removes the possibility of blocking cluster state updates as a result of them waiting
on the write-lock which might take a long time if a slow read operation executes concurrently.

Closes #63586

NOTE: I ran almost 10k iterations of all searchable snapshot integ tests over this one without failure, this change also visibly speeds up tests.
pr_comments: @tlrx I think this is good for review now. I simplified it a little more and added some more comments. The test failure is not related to this PR but some dep download thing we currently see in master as well. Hope this makes sense :)

> I wonder if it was possible to write a test that provokes the issue of #63586 with higher certainty?

I suppose technically we could construct the scenario that lead to this issue by some tricky blocking of repository reads at just the right points. But I'm not sure we want that:
1. That would be a significant effort and would only be a relevant special case in the old code, not in the new code this PR introduces.
2. We can probably make it much more likely to shake out this kind of issue and others similar to it by just more aggressively testing concurrent search + relocate which is the actual thing that caused trouble here but I'm not sure how far we want to go here. It's always a trade-off between making the tests slower and increasing the chance of catching things I guess and I'd have a hard time at guessing better parameters for parallelism etc. than what we're currently working with.

Yeah, it is tricky. I was thinking that we could have a test of just `CacheFile`, calling `acquire`, `release`, `startEviction`, `populateAndRead` in multiple threads (in legal ways), with some level of blocking in the `reader` and `writer` passed to `populateAndRead`.

@henningandersen I think I found a way of getting reasonable coverage without too much effort :) I pushed 3c3756af25d where I used the deterministic thread pool to simulate a number of possible permutations of adding and releasing a listener while concurrently evicting the file. This actually tracked down a real-world bug (that was obvious in hindsight but would only show on Windows ... or using `WindowsFS` as in this case:)) that is fixed in the same commit.
I could potentially extend that test a little to use more eviction listeners for example if you want (not sure how much that actually changes, it covers most possible logical scenarios as far as I can tell) and maybe that's all the coverage we need?

Thanks for the review @henningandersen I think I addressed all your comments now :) (also ran a few thousand iterations of the tests with the latest changes to releasing the file reference and it still seems to run fine.

review_comments: We can't assert that. We could still be using that specific channel in a background operation. This fact is to some degree at the heart of what motivated this PR: we don't want to lock here and wait for all the background fetchers/warmers etc. to be done with the file so we don't have to block and instead have the last of them to finish its work close it.
Thanks, I wonder if we should then just change the comment a few lines up to not say "close" (or just remove the comment), at least that is what confused me.

Related to your discussion below I believe we could add:
```
assert false : "expected a non-closed channel reference"
```
Yea that seems like a safe thing to try :) thanks!

There's no need for a `volatile` and immutable set of listeners here. We never accessed the listeners outside of the lock so we can simply mutate them in place.
I made this clearer now by using the `listeners` set as the mutex for all operations that apply to the set and the channel opening/closing that is a result of the set size.

I found this a lot cleaner and easier to reason about than checking the value of this boolean twice with tricky locking and the cost of the atomic reference relative to the `volatile` boolean should be trivial.

This lock seems pointless to me and was causing trouble. If an eviction of the current file is concurrently started, all that happened here was that we would block that eviction when as far as I can tell we should simply fail the cache population as it's just wasted effort anyway as soon as the eviction hits?

Looking at this again I think that `gap.onCompletion();` should be executed within the try/finally block, before the reference is decremented, as completing the gap might trigger the execution of some listeners.

I think we have this covered by the fact that we increment the reference by one anyway in `getFileChannelReference` so unless we are in some broken state where the overall listener got failed async (maybe that's impossible even?) the ref counting here is actually redundant.
I actually added the ref counting in `getFileChannelReference` to cover this exact spot so we're not without a reference when completing the listener. (I suppose we could do away with the incrementing in `getFileChannelReference` and decrementing after if we made this change, but it seemed easier to reason about the way it currently is but maybe that's just me?)
Yes, sorry, I've been puzzled a minute by the decRef following by the gap's completion instead of the other way around... sorry for the noise you can ignore my comment.

Same argument as in the other spot where I removed use of this method, what's the point of locking here when all we do is make the cache file be used after eviction has already been started, meaning all the writes going into it are wasted anyway?

The point was to keep the file around in order to be able to process any concurrent read operation (if any) that would have required a gap to be filled. But there was no reason to prevent other listeners to be acquired nor an eviction to kick in. Your change improves all of that.

This seems unchanged, but I find it slightly odd to have both the option of returning false from this method as well as throwing `AlreadyClosedException` when this `CacheFile` is being evicted. Am I missing something here?

Yea I'm not sure about this either. I think we should just always throw here, since the only way we could conceivably return `false` is if we evict between `ensureOpen()` and trying to increment the ref counter (which is close to impossible).
Maybe change that in a follow-up though, could simplify this and also the `release` method which always returns `true` currently as well and can be simplified to a `void`.

Yes, I think this is a left over when the IndexInput tried to re-acquire a cache file if it failed to add itself as a listener. I guess we were just returning `false` at that time in case of eviction.

Anyway, I'm +1 on throwing.
